results.title: Versioning, Provenance, and Reproducibility - Machine Learning in Production: From Models to Products
results.content: When building systems with machine-learning components, responsible engineers usually aim to version data, ML pipeline code, models, non-ML code, and possibly infrastructure configurations. These experiment tracking tools usually provide higher-level APIs that are called from within data science code to upload new versions of a model to the dashboard. **Logging custom metadata.** Developers can add instructions to their pipeline code to produce provenance metadata for every data transformation, logging what data is read, what version of what code is run, and what data is written as a result, usually tracking exact file paths and versions or file hashes. Moveover, pipeline automation frameworks or data science platforms can provide integrated versioning and provenance tracking support for the entire machine-learning pipeline, possibly all the way to deployed models—leaving only the integration of the application with the various versioned models to developers. Provenance tracking follows the flow of data through various processing steps and files, often integrated with pipeline automation tools, and facilitates this connection of various versions of data and code artifacts.

results.content: An example of a publish workflow is as follows: `1# ./.github/workflows/publish.yml 12 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 15 id-token: write # needed for provenance data generation 19 uses: actions/checkout@v4 25 uses: actions/setup-node@v4 34 - name: Print Environment Info 35 run: npx nx report 39 run: npx nx release publish This workflow will install node, install npm dependencies, then run `nx release publish` to publish the packages. Note: The `NPM_ACCESS_TOKEN` name is not important other than that it matches the usage in the workflow: 2 run: npx nx release publish ### NPM Provenance To verify your packages with npm provenance, set the `NPM_CONFIG_PROVENANCE` environment variable to `true` in the step where `nx release publish` is performed. The workflow will also need the `id-token: write` permission to generate the provenance data: 4 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 7 id-token: write # needed for provenance data generation 2 run: npx nx release publish ## Publishing Docker Images (Experimental) Docker support in Nx is currently experimental and may undergo breaking changes without following semantic versioning. ### Docker Registry Authentication Before publishing Docker images, ensure you're authenticated with your Docker registry: `1- name: Login to Docker Hub 2 uses: docker/login-action@v2 7- name: Build and tag Docker images 8 run: npx nx release version --dockerVersionScheme=production 10- name: Publish Docker images 11 run: npx nx release publish For changelogs, you can run `npx nx release changelog <version>` locally with the new version from the pipeline. ### Using Different Registries Configure alternative registries in your `nx.json`: 4 "registryUrl": "ghcr.io" // GitHub Container Registry ### Example GitHub Actions Workflow for Docker 9 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 11 - uses: actions/checkout@v3 13 - name: Setup Node.js 14 uses: actions/setup-node@v3 22 run: npx nx run-many -t build 24 - name: Login to Docker Hub 25 uses: docker/login-action@v2 30 - name: Build and tag Docker images 31 run: npx nx release version --dockerVersionScheme=production 33 - name: Publish Docker images 34 run: npx nx release publish #### Guides * Release TypeScript/JavaScript Packages to NPM * Updating Version References in Manifest Files (e.g. package.json) * Automatically Version with Conventional Commits * File Based Versioning (Version Plans) * Update Your Local Registry Setup to use Nx Release * Configuring Version Prefix for Dependency Versions #### Reference

results.title: How do you manage dependencies in a CI pipeline? | by AL.Eniyan | Medium
results.content: # How do you manage dependencies in a CI pipeline? Managing dependencies in a **Continuous Integration (CI)** pipeline is a critical part of ensuring the consistency, reliability, and reproducibility of builds. Here’s a comprehensive guide on how to manage dependencies in a CI pipeline:. * **Node.js (JavaScript/TypeScript)**: Use `npm` or `yarn` for managing dependencies. * Example: `npm install` or `yarn install` installs dependencies from `package.json`. * **Python**: Use `pip` and `requirements.txt` or `pipenv` to manage dependencies. Make sure that **dependency management files** (like `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `Gemfile`, etc.) are committed to your source control system (e.g., Git). Automating Dependency Installation in CI Pipeline:. Each CI pipeline (like **Jenkins**, **GitHub Actions**, **GitLab CI**, **CircleCI**, or **Travis CI**) should have steps to automatically install dependencies before running tests or **building the project.** Here’s an example of how to handle dependencies in a CI pipeline:. on: push: branches: [main]jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v2 - name: Set up Node.js uses: actions/setup-node@v2 with: node-version: '14' - name: Install dependencies run: npm install - name: Run tests run: npm test. * The pipeline installs dependencies using `npm install` (or `yarn install`). To improve build performance, you can **cache dependencies** between pipeline runs. Caching avoids downloading and installing dependencies on every pipeline execution, saving time. Ensure that dependencies are fixed to specific versions to avoid unexpected issues due to newer versions being installed in different pipeline runs. Pinning the exact version (e.g., using `npm install --save-exact`) ensures that all environments use the same versions of the dependencies. To avoid **security vulnerabilities** and outdated dependencies, regularly update your dependencies and run security checks as part of the CI pipeline. Docker allows you to build an image that contains all your dependencies and then run your CI tests in that image. In this case, you build a Docker image with your app and its dependencies, and then run tests inside that container, ensuring consistency across environments. In a CI pipeline, managing dependencies involves:. * **Using dependency managers** (like npm, pip, Maven, etc.) to install dependencies. By handling dependencies carefully in your **CI pipeline,** you ensure that builds are consistent, reliable, and secure every time a change is made.

results.title: Solving Reproducibility & Transparency in Google Cloud Build CI/CD Pipelines - ActiveState
results.content: ## Solving Reproducibility & Transparency in Google Cloud Build CI/CD Pipelines. * build engineering, ci cd pipeline, CI/CD, Code Provenance, Google Cloud Build, Reproducibility. When it comes to CI/CD, most vendors support containers as an option to either contain the base execution environment, or as a way of storing the artifacts created at the end of the pipeline, but Google Cloud Build (GCB) is a “container-native” product which is literally built on top of a container pipeline. As a container-only solution, GCB takes advantage of Google’s Cloud infrastructure to execute builds faster and cheaper. **The result is a more secure and compliant Google Cloud Build CI/CD pipeline. Google has gone all-in on container technology when building its Google Cloud Platform, so it’s no surprise that its CI/CD offering leverages containers, as well. So, without further ado, let’s set up a Python runtime environment in Google Cloud Build and execute some tests in a containerized CI pipeline. Once again, I’ll be using a sample application (the same one I used in my previous CI/CD blog posts) written in Python and hosted on GitHub. GitHub will be our source of truth for the code, and we’ll use the ActiveState Platform as the source of truth for the runtime environment, which includes a version of Python and all the packages the GitHub project requires (note that the process here is just as valid for Perl projects/runtimes, as well). GCB will grab the runtime from the ActiveState Platform and the source code from GitHub, and then build and run its tests for a successful round of development iteration. If you create a private project on the ActiveState Platform, you’ll need to create a secret for your credentials via Google’s Secret Manager, similar to the API key instructions below. * Integrate GCB with the ActiveState Platform using State Cloud Builder’s built-in authentication for Secret Manager. ## Integrating Google Cloud Build with the ActiveState Platform. **As a result, the ActiveState Platform ensures your projects can be built (and rebuilt at any point in time) in a secure, consistent manner, while providing visibility into the CI/CD pipeline and improving the traceability of production workloads.**.
